Delegate Bartlett expressed his intention to do all he can to prevent approval of the order which would cut between $360,000 and $400,000 yearly from Federal pay checks in Juneau alone. Alaska's Delegate is working on the matter in conjunction with the Delegate to Congress from Hawaii, Joseph R. Harrington.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa.—(NNPA)

Morgan State, Colored Intercollegiate conference champions for the past four years, defeated Lincoln University, 90-0 before a crowd of 5000 in Shibe Park last Friday night.

The superior power and line play of Morgan asserted itself in the second half, after being held scoreless in the first half.

JACKIE ROBINSON, former Kansas Monarchs shortstop, who signed contract with the Brooklyn Dodgers, was an honorary referee during part of the game.

Appearing in Philadelphia for the first time, Morgan put the score on the ice in the first minute of the second half. Art Berry, halfback, knitted 15 yards in one 3-man tackle for the first and second who shifted from end to fullback, got the last one on a one-yard plunge through left guard to the end on a 46-yard drive.

Washington, Feb. 12—INS—A reported Soviet request for a ten billion dollar credit from the United States for postwar reconstruction was the subject of wide comment in official Washington circles to-day.

Previous reports had mentioned a six billion dollar Soviet request.

Purpose of the loan, officials said, was to make possible a continued flow of American goods to Russia, after lend-lease was terminated with the end of the war.

Yugoslavia has been an area of joint Soviet British influence, but the Soviet influence is increasing. Dominant Soviet political influence in Poland has increased with the almost complete occupation of that country by the Red Army.

United Press (Staff Correspondent)

Chicago, Oct. 16 (UP)—When the American Legion convenes here Nov. 18-25 it probably will be addressed for the first time in its 27 years of life by a President of the United States who is a veteran of World War I.

Tentative plans call for the appearance of President Harry S. Truman, former artillery officer, to head the list of speakers at the organization's first postwar convention. It brings to the limelight the fact that after no other war did almost three decades pass before a veteran became the nation's Chief Executive.

The President, long an active legionnaire, will be cast in a different role, too. For years he has attended Legion conventions as a delegate of the Department of Missouri. This time he will be the organization's honored guest.

New High In Members

The Legion will come to Chicago with an all-high mark in membership, according to national headquarters at Indianapolis—670,000 strong, including half a million veterans of World War II, and with predictions by Legion leaders that it will close with a membership of approximately 3,000,000.

A record number of delegates in excess of 2,000 with each representing approximately 800 members, will be on hand for the fourth national Convention to be held in Chicago. Previous occasions were 1883, 1899 and 1944.

Although the next national convention will break all records for delegates strength, housing accommodations will limit the non-delegate attendance. It will be impossible to find lodging for the hundreds of thousands of members who attended conventions in prewar years.

It is anticipated that younger legionnaires who are veterans of World War II will have candidates for national offices which, it was felt in some quarters, may bring about a change of pace for older leaders who in the past aspired to and sometimes attained the role of "King Makers" in connection with national positions.

U. S. Welfare Keynote

It was known well in advance that department conventions have elected many younger veterans as delegates to the national meeting and that the youngsters took leading part in discussing and drafting resolutions to be presented to the national body.

The keynote of the convention will be the welfare of America and the millions of returning fighting men of World War II, according to Commander Edward N. who will close his term of office with the distinction of having served longer than any other national commander. This is because wartime restrictions caused a 14-month period to span conventions whereas in the past it was only one year.

All phases of problems confronting veterans will form the main business of the convention, according to national headquarters. This will range from disqualification and allied matters, to a demand that there be no release of conscientious objectors until all combat veterans, aside from professional soldiers and regular servicemen and women have been discharged.
